0.title: Help My Unbelief
0.essay:
Many Christians struggle with doubt, and many are ashamed to admit it. They wonder whether God is really there, whether the Bible is really true, whether they are really saved, or why God seems silent when they pray.

Hidden doubts

Some keep their doubts hidden for years, afraid of what others would think. Some drift from the faith because no one helped them. Yet Scripture is surprisingly honest about doubt. The Psalms are full of questions. John the Baptist, in prison, sent to ask Jesus whether he really was the one. Thomas refused to believe without seeing. A desperate father cried out to Jesus, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). And Jesus did not turn any of them away.

Doubt is not unbelief

Doubt is faith struggling; unbelief is faith refused. A believer can doubt and still belong to Christ, because salvation rests not on the strength of our faith but on the strength of the Saviour we trust. Even weak faith in a strong Christ saves.

The chapters

Honest Doubt in Scripture; Kinds of Doubt; When God Seems Silent; Unanswered Prayer; and Strengthening Faith. The Apologetics study takes up intellectual questions about the faith in more depth.

1.title: Honest Doubt in Scripture
1.essay:
The Bible does not hide the struggles of God’s people. Habakkuk cried, “O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear?” (Habakkuk 1:2). Asaph almost slipped when he saw the wicked prosper (Psalm 73:2–3). Gideon asked for sign after sign (Judges 6). Elijah, after his greatest victory, sat under a tree and asked to die (1 Kings 19:4). These were not unbelievers. They were saints whose faith was being tested.

A prophet’s complaint

Habakkuk complained that God was not listening and not acting against injustice: “So the law is paralyzed, and justice never goes forth” (Habakkuk 1:4). That is a prophet speaking, in Scripture. God allows honest complaint, and, as the rest of the book shows, he answers it.

John in prison

John the Baptist had baptised Jesus, seen the Spirit descend and called him the Lamb of God. But in Herod’s prison, waiting for death, he sent his disciples to ask, “Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?” (Matthew 11:3). Jesus did not rebuke him. He sent back evidence, the fulfilment of Isaiah’s prophecies: the blind see, the lame walk, the dead are raised, the poor hear good news. And he added a gentle word: “blessed is the one who is not offended by me” (Matthew 11:6). Then he praised John to the crowd (Matthew 11:11). Jesus does not always do what we expect, but he is still the one.

Help my unbelief

A man brought his son, tormented by an evil spirit, to Jesus. “But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.” Jesus took up his words: “‘If you can’! All things are possible for one who believes.” And the father cried out, “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:22–24). His request was half faith and half doubt. The issue was not Jesus’ ability but the man’s trust. His honest cry is a prayer every believer can pray, and Jesus answered it by healing his son. Mixed faith, honestly brought to Jesus, was enough.

Lord, save me

After Jesus walked on the water, Peter asked to come to him. He stepped out and walked, but when he saw the wind he was afraid, and began to sink. He cried, “Lord, save me.” “Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him” (Matthew 14:30–31). Peter doubted, but he cried out, and Jesus caught him.

Thomas

Thomas refused to believe the resurrection unless he could touch Jesus’ wounds. A week later Jesus appeared and invited him to do exactly that. Thomas confessed, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). Jesus met Thomas in his doubt and led him to the highest confession in the Gospels. Then he blessed “those who have not seen and yet have believed” (John 20:29). That includes us. We have the testimony of those who saw, written “so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (John 20:31).

Mercy for doubters

Jude tells the church, “And have mercy on those who doubt” (Jude 22). Doubting believers need patience, not condemnation.

A woman who has been a Christian for twenty years confesses to her small group that she has had serious doubts for months. She fears they will be shocked. Instead two others admit they have struggled too. They study the Psalms together and pray for each other. Her faith does not return overnight, but she is no longer alone.

What faith is

Scripture warns against “an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God” (Hebrews 3:12). That is the settled refusal to trust. Doubt is different: a mind and heart torn between faith and fear. The doubter still turns to God with questions; the unbeliever turns away.

Faith is not a feeling of certainty but trust in God and his promises. You can trust while feeling uncertain, as a nervous patient trusts a surgeon. And what saves is not the size of our faith but its object. A small faith in Christ unites us to him as truly as a great one. Jesus said that faith “like a grain of mustard seed” is enough (Matthew 17:20).

Have you ever been afraid to admit your doubts to another Christian? Why?

For reflection

Which biblical example of doubt do you identify with most, and why? What is the difference between doubt and unbelief? How did Jesus respond to doubters, and what does that tell you about him? Is there someone struggling with doubt to whom you could show mercy?

2.title: Kinds of Doubt
2.essay:
Doubt comes in different forms, and each needs a different kind of help. Faith involves the whole person — mind, heart and will — and doubts can arise in any of them.

Intellectual doubt

Some doubts are questions about evidence and argument. Is the Bible reliable? Did Jesus really rise? Why does God allow suffering? How does faith relate to science? These questions deserve honest answers, and Christianity is not afraid of them. Luke “followed all things closely for some time past” and wrote an orderly account “that you may have certainty concerning the things you have been taught” (Luke 1:3–4). Christianity is grounded in history and evidence. Faith is not a leap in the dark.

Peter insisted, “For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty” (2 Peter 1:16). And beyond the eyewitnesses we have the prophetic word, spoken by men “carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21). Good books, wise teachers and patient study help.

A university student begins to doubt the resurrection after a sceptical lecture. A Christian friend gives her a careful book on the evidence and studies 1 Corinthians 15 with her. Her questions are taken seriously, and over time her faith becomes stronger than before, because it has been tested.

Emotional doubt

Some doubts are driven by feelings, not arguments. In depression, grief, anxiety or exhaustion, God can feel unreal or far away, even when we know the truth. The psalmist speaks to his own soul: “Why are you cast down, O my soul?” (Psalm 42:5). Emotional doubt needs rest, care, honest lament and the reminder that feelings are not facts.

Asaph could not sleep and felt that God had rejected him. He asked painful questions: “Will the Lord spurn forever, and never again be favorable? Has his steadfast love forever ceased?” (Psalm 77:7–8). Then he chose to remember: “I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your wonders of old” (Psalm 77:11). He meditated on the exodus and God’s redemption of his people. Memory of God’s past faithfulness strengthened his faith for the present. Remembering is a weapon against doubt.

Doubt from suffering

Some doubts arise from pain: a child’s death, a long illness, an injustice. Why would a loving God allow this? These doubts need comfort before arguments. Job’s friends tried to explain; Job needed God himself.

Doubt about salvation

Some believers doubt not God but themselves. Am I really saved? Have I committed the unforgivable sin? Is my faith real? These doubts need the gospel: salvation rests on Christ’s finished work, not on the strength of our feelings. The Assurance of Salvation study takes this up.

Doubt from sin

Sometimes doubt is a cover for something else. Someone who wants to live in sin may find reasons to doubt God’s word. Jesus said, “If anyone’s will is to do God’s will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority” (John 7:17). Willingness to obey opens the way to understanding. Sometimes doubt is resolved by surrender, not only by study, and honest self-examination is part of dealing with it.

The Spirit and the church

In the end, certainty about God comes not from arguments alone but from the Spirit’s work. “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Romans 8:16). Arguments can remove obstacles; the Spirit gives conviction.

And doubt grows in isolation. The church carries its members’ faith when they cannot carry it themselves. “But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called ‘today’” (Hebrews 3:13).

If you have doubts, what kind are they: intellectual, emotional, from suffering, about your salvation, or from sin?

For reflection

Which kind of doubt do you struggle with most? How does Luke 1:1–4 show that Christianity is grounded in history? Read Psalm 77: how did remembering help Asaph? Is there any area where your doubts might be connected to an unwillingness to obey?

3.title: When God Seems Silent
3.essay:
One of the hardest experiences in the Christian life is when God seems absent. Prayers seem to hit the ceiling. Bible reading feels dry. There is no sense of his presence. Many believers have walked through such seasons.

The psalmists knew it

“How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?” (Psalm 13:1). David asks “How long?” four times. He feels forgotten, abandoned and in danger. He asks God to answer and give light. Then, with no explanation and no change of circumstances recorded, he turns: “But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation” (Psalm 13:5). He resolves to sing. His decision to trust came before his feelings changed. Lament can lead to trust, even before circumstances change.

Psalm 88 ends with no resolution at all: “my companions have become darkness” (Psalm 88:18). God included such prayers in Scripture so that we would know we are not alone, and so that we would have words to pray when we have none.

Walking in darkness

Isaiah gives counsel for such times: “Who among you fears the LORD and obeys the voice of his servant? Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God” (Isaiah 50:10). Notice that this person fears God and obeys, and yet walks in darkness. Darkness is not proof of God’s displeasure. The answer is not to wait for feelings but to trust God’s name and lean on him. And Isaiah warns against lighting our own fires (Isaiah 50:11) — making our own light rather than waiting on God. In darkness, the temptation is to find substitutes. The answer is to trust.

Job could not find him

“Behold, I go forward, but he is not there, and backward, but I do not perceive him” (Job 23:8). Job searched in every direction and could not find God. “But he knows the way that I take; when he has tried me, I shall come out as gold” (Job 23:10). He could not see God, but he believed God could see him. And he had treasured God’s words “more than my portion of food” (Job 23:12). He held to God’s word when he could not feel God’s presence.

Keep using the means

In dry seasons, keep praying, reading Scripture, going to church and taking the Lord’s Supper, even when it feels empty. Feelings often return later. Meanwhile the means of grace are doing their quiet work.

A missionary who has served faithfully for decades goes through a long season in which God feels distant. She keeps praying the Psalms, even when they feel empty. She tells a friend, “I can’t feel him, but I know he’s there.” Years later she describes that season as the time her faith grew deepest.

Christ was forsaken

Darkness covered the land as Jesus hung on the cross, and he cried out with the opening words of Psalm 22: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). The Son experienced real abandonment as he bore our sin. He was truly forsaken so that his people never will be. When God seems silent to us, we can remember that he was silent to his Son, for our sake. And he has promised, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

Presence and feelings

God is always present with his people: “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Our sense of his presence varies. Believers have long spoken of seasons when God seems to withdraw the felt sense of his nearness, to test and deepen faith. His actual presence never leaves. “For we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7), and faith that keeps going in darkness is precious to him.

Dry seasons can have many causes: tiredness, illness, depression, unconfessed sin, or simply God’s mysterious purposes. Wise counsel helps tell which.

If God feels distant right now, which psalm could you pray as your own?

For reflection

Have you known a season when God seemed silent, and what helped you? Read Psalm 88: why do you think God included a psalm with no happy ending? What does Isaiah 50:10 tell you to do in darkness? How does Christ’s cry of abandonment comfort you?

4.title: Unanswered Prayer
4.essay:
Few things shake faith like unanswered prayer. A believer prays for healing, and the person dies. A couple pray for a child for years, and none comes. A parent prays for a prodigal who never returns. Where is God?

God always hears

“And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us” (1 John 5:14). God hears every prayer of his children. But he answers according to his will, which is wiser than ours.

Sometimes the answer is no

Paul pleaded three times for his thorn to be removed. God said no, and gave something better: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Paul learned to boast in his weaknesses. A refused prayer became a gateway to a deeper experience of Christ’s strength.

Even Jesus prayed three times in Gethsemane, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). The Father did not remove the cup. And because of that unanswered request, our salvation was accomplished. The greatest prayer ever refused brought about the greatest good. Jesus models both honest prayer and complete submission.

Sometimes it is wait

Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac. Hannah prayed for years for a child, so earnestly in the temple that the priest thought she was drunk. She poured out her soul, God answered, and she bore Samuel; her song of praise afterwards is one of the great prayers of Scripture (1 Samuel 1–2). Jesus told a parable “to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart” (Luke 18:1). If an unjust judge eventually gives a persistent widow justice, how much more will God give justice to his chosen ones who cry to him day and night? Delay is not denial. And Jesus ends with a searching question: “Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8).

Sometimes it is different

God may answer in ways we do not recognise at first. We ask for comfort and he gives strength; we ask for removal and he gives endurance.

Sometimes we ask wrongly

“You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions” (James 4:3). Some prayers go unanswered because they are selfish or contrary to God’s will.

All things for good

When we do not know how to pray, “the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26), according to God’s will. And “we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28). That does not mean all things are good. It means God weaves even our disappointments into his good purpose, which is to conform us “to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29), and he will bring every one of his people to glory. Unanswered prayers are part of that purpose.

A false gospel of prayer

Some teach that if we have enough faith, God must give us health and wealth. That is not biblical. Paul had great faith and was not healed. Faith trusts God’s will; it does not command him.

Prayer is still real and powerful: “The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working” (James 5:16). God has chosen to accomplish many things through the prayers of his people. But prayer is always subject to his wiser will.

Lament

When prayers go unanswered, Scripture permits lament: honest complaint brought to God. Lament is still prayer, still faith, still turning to God rather than away.

A couple prayed for years for their son’s healing, but he died young. Their faith was shaken. Over many months, through lament, the support of their church and the promise of resurrection, they came to trust God again. They still do not know why. But they know who, and they believe they will see their son again.

Is there an unanswered prayer that has shaken your faith? Have you brought that disappointment honestly to God?

For reflection

Which unanswered prayer has been hardest for you? How does Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane help you understand unanswered prayer? What is the difference between “no”, “wait” and “a different answer”? How do Romans 8:28–29 help you trust God when prayers are not answered as you hoped?

5.title: Strengthening Faith
5.essay:
Faith is a gift from God, but it can be strengthened. “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8). We do not manufacture faith. We receive it, and ask for more. And Scripture shows how it grows.

Hear God’s word

Paul traces a chain: people cannot call on one they have not believed in, or believe in one they have not heard of, or hear without a preacher. “So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17). The word of God is the ordinary means by which faith is born and grows. The Gospels were written “so that you may believe” (John 20:31). Doubters should not stop reading the Bible; they should read it more.

A man struggling with doubt begins reading one Gospel chapter every morning, asking, “What does this show me about Jesus?” He also keeps a list of answered prayers and God’s kindnesses. Over a year his faith steadies. Not all his questions have been answered, but his trust in Christ is stronger.

Look to Jesus

Hebrews 11 calls faith “the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen”, and says that “without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him” (Hebrews 11:1, 6). Then it lists people who trusted God’s promises without seeing them fulfilled — Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses and many more. “These all died in faith, not having received the things promised” (Hebrews 11:13).

That great cloud of witnesses encourages us to run with endurance. But the main focus is Jesus: “looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2). “Consider him … so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted” (Hebrews 12:3). Faith grows by looking at its object, not by examining itself. The more we see of Christ — his character, his cross, his resurrection — the more we trust him.

Remember

Israel set up stones by the Jordan so that their children would ask what they meant, and hear what God had done (Joshua 4). Remembering God’s faithfulness, in Scripture and in our own lives, strengthens faith for the present.

Stay in fellowship, obey, and pray

Believers strengthen one another; the faith of others, past and present, encourages ours. Faith also grows through obedience. When we step out in trust, we see God’s faithfulness, and our faith grows. And it is right to ask for more of it. The apostles said to Jesus, “Increase our faith!” (Luke 17:5).

Tested faith

Peter says trials come “so that the tested genuineness of your faith—more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire—may be found to result in praise and glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:7). Doubt and testing can refine faith rather than destroy it.

Held by Christ

“I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). God wants his children to be sure. And our security rests not on our grip on Christ but on his grip on us. “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:27–28). No one can snatch them from the Father’s hand either. The security of believers rests on Christ’s power and promise, not on the steadiness of their feelings.

And he prays for us. Jesus prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), and “he always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25). Our faith is upheld by his intercession.

Which of these ways of strengthening faith could you practise this week?

For reflection

Which means of strengthening faith do you most neglect? How does “looking to Jesus” differ from looking at your own faith? Make a list of ways God has been faithful to you: how does it affect your faith? Read John 10:27–30. How does it comfort you in times of doubt?
